welcome.title: Welcome to Shading
body: This tutorial builds a short animation together with you, one step at a time. Blocks are placed for you as you press **Next** — feel free to click them, change numbers and experiment along the way.
The tutorial uses effect blocks from the official plugins, so they need to be installed first.

renderFrame.title: The render frame block
body: A video is a series of still pictures called frames — 30 every second by default. `render frame` in **Events** runs the script below it once for every frame, from the top, and whatever those blocks draw becomes that frame.
Instead of moving sprites around, you describe what the picture looks like at the current time. Press **Next** to place the block.

renderFramePlaced.title: Your first script
body: `render frame` is now in the code area. Everything attached below it runs on every frame: while playing, while you scrub the timeline, and when the video is rendered.
Next, let's draw something.

objects.title: Objects: things to draw
body: The **Objects** category holds the blocks that draw:

list: `draw` — costumes, text, videos and 3D models
`shape` — polygons, stars, flowers and other shapes
`arc` and `circular segment` — rings, pie slices and arcs
`line` — a line between two points in 3D

body: Blocks run from top to bottom, so what is drawn later appears in front.

drawMedia.title: The draw block and media
body: The first menu of `draw` chooses what to draw. It lists the costumes, videos, fonts and 3D models of this project.

Press **Import** in that menu to load an image, video, font or 3D model straight from your computer — you can also drop or paste files onto it, or put several costumes together into a sequence. Media can also be managed in the tabs on the left.
For text, the menu chooses the font: Sans Serif, Serif, Monospace, or any font you added. Press **Next** to draw the text “Hello Shading!”.

drawPlaced.title: Hello Shading!
body: The text appears on the stage. These are the values of `draw`:

list: **text** — the words to draw
**italic** — slants the letters (0 is upright, negative numbers lean left)
**position x / y / z** — where it is in 3D: x to the right, y up, z away from the camera. At z = 480, 1 equals one pixel of the stage.
**rotation x / y / z** — turns it around each axis, in degrees
**scale x / y / z** — stretches it along each axis (1 is the original size)
**size** — the overall size in % (50 here)
**width / height** — stretches the picture sideways / up and down, in %
**time** — from when to when (in seconds) it is drawn. Infinity means until the end.

body: Try changing a value — the stage updates right away.

camera.title: The camera
body: Everything you draw is filmed by a virtual camera. The **Camera** category moves and turns it: move the camera and the whole view moves, just like with a real camera.
Press **Next** to put `set camera to x: y: z:` at the top of the script.

cameraPlaced.title: Setting the camera
body: `set camera to x: 0 y: 0 z: 0` now runs before `draw`, so the text is filmed from this position. Always set the camera before the blocks that draw.

list: **x** — moves the camera to the right (negative: to the left)
**y** — moves it up (negative: down)
**z** — moves it forward. The camera looks toward +z, so the text at z = 480 is 480 in front of it.

body: Try typing 240 into z: the camera moves closer and the text gets bigger. Set it back to 0 afterwards.

operators.title: Operators
body: **Operators** calculate values: + − × ÷, random numbers, comparisons (> < =), and / or / not, joining text, and math functions such as sin, cos and abs. They fit into any round slot.
Shading adds `easing`: a number that changes smoothly over time. It is the main way to animate things.

easing.title: The easing block
body: This is `easing`. Let's use it to make the camera fly in.
Press **Next** to put an easing block into the camera's z.

easingPlaced.title: Easing values
body: The camera's z is now `easing`:

list: **type** — the shape of the motion. *In* starts slowly, *Out* ends slowly, *InOut* does both; Power, Circ and Expo are different curves. Here: PowerOut.
**Elastic / Bounce**, **speed** and **strength** — add a wobble on top. Speed 0 turns it off.
**value 480 ~ 0** — the value at the start and at the end
**time 0 ~ 1.5** — when the change happens, in seconds. Before 0 s it is 480; after 1.5 s it stays at 0.
**power 3** — how strong the curve is (larger means sharper)

body: The camera now starts right at the text and pulls back in 1.5 seconds. Press ▶ on the timeline to watch it.

timeline.title: The timeline
body: The timeline controls time:

list: ▶ plays and pauses (Space). ■ stops and goes back to 0 s (Shift+Space).
Click or drag on the ruler to jump to any moment. The frame is rebuilt for that time right away.
**Keyframe** marks an important time (K). Blocks can read it with `keyframe [1] time`.
⚙ opens the rendering settings, and **?** lists every keyboard shortcut.

body: The time shown here is the time that `easing` and `timer` use. Drag the playhead between 0 and 1.5 s to see the camera move frame by frame.

combine.title: Easings are just numbers
body: An easing block is a value, so you can do math with it. Let's add two of them:

list: PowerIn, value 0 ~ 100, time 0 ~ 1
PowerOut, value 0 ~ 100, time 1 ~ 2

body: The sum goes 0 → 100 during the first second and 100 → 200 during the next — two moves in one value. Press **Next** to put it into the text's position x.

combinePlaced.title: Two moves in one value
body: The text now speeds up to the right and then glides to a stop. Each easing only changes during its own time range and holds its value outside it, so you can add more with + to choreograph longer motions.

variables.title: Variables
body: A variable stores one value under a name.

list: **Make a Variable** in the **Variables** category creates one. “For all sprites” can be used everywhere; “For this sprite only” belongs to this sprite.
`set [ ] to` stores a value, `change [ ] by` adds to it, and the round reporter with its name reads it.

lists.title: Lists
body: A list holds many values in order.

list: **Make a List** creates one.
`add [ ] to`, `insert [ ] at`, `replace item` and `delete` change it.
`item ( ) of`, `item # of`, `length of` and `contains` read it.
`delete all of` empties it.

body: Lists are handy for data that belongs together, such as a color or a position for each letter.

tmp.title: Variables as temporary values
body: The render frame script starts from the top on every frame, so in Shading variables are mostly used as temporary values (“tmp”): calculate something once near the top, then use it wherever you need it below.
Lists work the same way: `delete all of` at the top, then `add` what you need for this frame.
Press **Next** to store our x motion in a variable called tmp.

tmpPlaced.title: Using tmp
body: `set tmp to` now calculates the motion once, and `draw` reads (tmp). Anything else that should move the same way can use (tmp) too.
Set a temporary variable before the blocks that read it — otherwise they see the value from the previous frame.

grouping.title: Grouping
body: `grouping` turns everything drawn in its top slot into one layer. Effects placed in its bottom slot (**effects**) apply only to that layer.
Press **Next** to put the text into a grouping and add a red `color overlay` to its effects.

groupingPlaced.title: Effects for one group
body: The text is inside `grouping`, and `color overlay` (red, mix 100%) in the effects slot paints only this group red.
Click the color to choose another one, or lower mix to blend it with the original colors.

looks.title: Looks: effects
body: The **Looks** category holds the effects that plugins add: blur, glow, color correction, distortion, film looks and more.

list: Placed directly in the render frame script, an effect applies to the whole picture drawn so far.
Placed in the effects slot of `grouping`, it applies only to that group — for example, blur the background but keep the title sharp.

costumes.title: The Costumes tab
body: The **Costumes** tab holds images. Paint them in the built-in editor, or upload SVG, PNG, JPG, GIF, WebP, EXR and more.
Choose a costume in the menu of `draw` to show it. In that menu you can also turn several costumes into a sequence and flip through them with frame.

sounds.title: The Sounds tab
body: The **Sounds** tab holds sounds: upload, record and edit them (WAV, MP3, OGG, FLAC, AAC, M4A).
To put a sound into the video, use `play sound at [ ] time: [ ] ~ [ ]` from the **Sound** category in the render frame script. It follows the timeline and is included when you render.

videos.title: The Videos tab
body: The **Videos** tab holds video clips (MP4, WebM, OGV, MOV). Draw them with `draw`:

list: **sequence** — frame chooses the picture (30 frames per second; frame 1 is the start)
**video** — plays in sync with the timeline, with its own speed and volume

fonts.title: The Fonts tab
body: The **Fonts** tab adds fonts (TTF, OTF, WOFF, WOFF2) and shows a preview. Added fonts appear in the text choices of `draw`.

models.title: The Models tab
body: The **Models** tab adds 3D models (GLB, PMX, FBX, OBJ + MTL) and motions or poses (VMD, VPD).
Draw a model with `draw` like any other object; frame plays its motion. Position, rotation and scale work in real 3D.

shader.title: The Shader tab
body: The **Shader** tab is for making your own effects. Write a WebGL fragment shader (GLSL), or upload a .glsl file or shader package.
Each shader becomes a block in **Looks**, and its uniforms become the block's inputs automatically.

pluginsTab.title: The Plugins tab
body: The **Plugins** tab lists the installed plugins. Turn each one on or off (after a reload), remove it, or add new ones from .zip files — also with the button at the bottom left of the code area.
Plugins run with the same permissions as the editor, so only install ones you trust. shading.app/install installs every official plugin at once.

blockShapes.title: Block shapes
body: Back to the code. A block's shape tells you where it fits:

list: **Hat blocks** (rounded top) start a script, like `render frame`.
**Stack blocks** do something. Their notches snap them together from top to bottom, like `draw`.
**C blocks** wrap other blocks, like `grouping`, `repeat` and `if`.
**Round reporters** are values — numbers or text — like `easing` or (tmp). They fit into round slots.
**Hexagonal booleans** are true or false, like `>` or `time within`. They fit into hexagonal slots such as the one in `if`.

timer.title: timer
body: `timer` in **Sensing** is the current time on the timeline, in seconds — while playing, scrubbing and rendering.
Multiply it for motion that never stops: (timer × 30) grows by 30 every second, so as an angle it turns 30° per second.

timeWithin.title: time within
body: `time within [ ] to [ ] sec` in **Objects** is true while the current time is inside the range.
Use it with `if` to show something only during part of the video, or to switch between scenes.

example.title: Let's build an animation
body: Now let's put everything together: the letters of “Hello Shading!” circle around the center, the camera flies in, the ring fades to red and a caption appears.
Press **Next** to build it. It replaces the tutorial's script.

examplePlaced.title: How it works
body: Press ▶ to watch it. From the top:

list: `set camera to` flies in with the easing from before.
`set tmp to` eases the radius of the circle from 0 to 120.
`set i to 1` and `set angle to (timer × 30)` prepare the loop. The timer makes the ring turn.
`repeat (length of Hello Shading!)` draws one letter per loop: `letter (i) of` picks it, sin and cos of angle place it on the circle, and rotation z tilts it along the circle.
`change i by 1` and `change angle by (360 / length)` move on to the next letter.
`color overlay` in the effects of `grouping` fades the ring to red between 2 and 3 s.
`if <time within 1.5 to 10 sec>` shows the caption from 1.5 s to the end. It is outside the group, so it does not turn red.

render.title: Rendering
body: When your animation is ready, render it into a video file.
Open the rendering settings with ⚙ on the timeline (or ⌘E / Ctrl+E).

renderSettings.title: Rendering settings

list: **Render preset** — quick settings: a 720p preview, or a 1080p / 4K final
**Export format** — MP4 video, transparent WebM, PNG sequence (.zip), the current frame as PNG, or audio only (WAV)
**Output width / height** — the size of the file. The stage keeps its size; this only changes the detail.
**Frame rate** — frames per second
**Max time** — the length of the video. **Range start / end** renders only part of it.
**Reuse unchanged frames** — keeps finished frames so rendering again is faster

body: This animation is 5 seconds long: set **Max time** to 5, then press **Render / export**. The video is downloaded when it's done.

finish.title: You did it!
body: You've finished the tutorial. You now know the basics of Shading: render frame, Objects, the camera, easing, the timeline, variables, grouping and effects, and rendering.
Keep experimenting with the animation you built. You can open this tutorial again any time from **Edit → Tutorial**.
